objective: By the end of this lesson you can diagnose partial power loss, electrical, instrument, gear, flap, trim, fire, icing and door problems from their first clues, choose the right POH checklist and action for each, and handle at least three of them on the checkride while keeping full control of the airplane.
why: Most malfunctions are not disasters by themselves; the accident usually comes from the pilot who stops flying the airplane to stare at the problem [[24:283|AFH 13-34]] [[24:366|AFH 18-17]]. As a commercial pilot you will carry people who trust you to know your airplane's systems well enough to tell a nuisance from an emergency, and to act on the manufacturer's procedures [[24:350|AFH 18-1]].

warmup: Think first: halfway through a cross-country the low-voltage light comes on, and a minute later the engine starts to run a little rough. Which problem do you work first, which checklist do you open, and what is the one thing you must keep doing the whole time?

key_terms.def: A POH procedure for a malfunction that is not considered an emergency. Some manufacturers put these in their own subsection of Section 3 [[1:234|PHAK 9-4]].
The first steps of an emergency checklist that you memorize and do before you read the checklist [[1:234|PHAK 9-4]].
A planned landing, on or off an airport, when you can still fly but should not, for example with developing engine trouble [[24:350|AFH 18-1]].
Uncontrolled, explosive burning of the fuel-air mixture in the cylinder, marked by high cylinder head temperature [[1:179|PHAK 7-19]].
The mixture lights before the spark plug fires, usually from a hot spot such as a carbon deposit or a cracked plug insulator [[1:179|PHAK 7-19]].
Turning off every electrical item you do not need after the alternator fails, so the battery lasts longer [[24:362|AFH 18-13]].
The bus a standby battery keeps alive in many glass cockpits: AHRS, air data computer, PFD, one nav and one com radio [[23:331|IFH 11-6]].
A combined display the system switches to when a screen fails, putting flight and engine data on the screen that still works [[23:329|IFH 11-4]].
A valve that lets the static instruments use cabin air pressure when the outside static port is blocked [[1:213|PHAK 8-11]].
One flap moves while the other stays put, giving a strong roll toward the wing with less flap [[24:360|AFH 18-11]].
A stall of an iced horizontal tail, most likely after full flap extension, that pitches the nose down [[38:27|AC 91-74B 3-7b]] [[38:52|AC 91-74B 5-12a]].
An automatic reflex (muscle jerk, racing heart, higher blood pressure) to a sudden, intense event you did not expect [[24:108|AFH 5-3]].

chunks.title: Malfunctions at the commercial level: the POH comes first

body.p: On the checkride the examiner picks at least three simulated emergencies from the knowledge list (power loss, system failures, smoke or fire, other systems, an open door) and watches you handle each one and finish the right checklist (ACS CA.IX.C.S1, CA.IX.C.S2). The private ACS lists the very same elements for this Task (ACS PA.IX.C). The difference at the commercial level is the job, not the list: you are training to carry people for hire, so expect the examiner to dig into how your own airplane's systems work and why each checklist step is there (application).
The FAA handbooks give only generic guidance. The procedures in your approved AFM/POH come first, and when the handbook and the manufacturer disagree, the manufacturer wins [[24:350|AFH 18-1]].

Section 3 of the POH, Emergency Procedures, holds the checklists for engine failure, fire and system failures. The short (abbreviated) checklist lists actions in the order you do them, and an amplified version follows with the reasons. Some POHs add an Abnormal Procedures subsection for malfunctions that are not emergencies. Memorize the immediate action items, then use the checklist [[1:234|PHAK 9-4]]. Procedures for optional equipment, such as an autopilot, live in Section 9, Supplements [[1:235|PHAK 9-5]].

Amplified procedure

callout.text: In an in-flight emergency that needs immediate action, the pilot in command may deviate from any rule of Part 91 as far as needed to meet it, and must send a written report if the FAA asks [[60:435|14 CFR 91.3]].

check.q: Where do you look first for the procedure for a failure in your airplane, and what do you do before reading it?
check.a: The POH/AFM Section 3 (or its Abnormal Procedures subsection, or a Section 9 supplement). Do the memorized immediate action items first, then use the checklist [[1:234|PHAK 9-4]] [[1:235|PHAK 9-5]].

chunks.title: Partial power loss: find the cause in an orderly way

body.p: Not every power problem is a broken engine. Many are fuel starvation, fixed by selecting another tank. An orderly check of gauges and switches often finds the cause: carburetor heat or alternate air, one magneto that runs smoother, a mixture change, or the boost pump if fuel vapor is suspected. Through all of it, keep flying the airplane; pilots have lost airplanes at altitude by fixating on the engine [[24:283|AFH 13-34]].

If there is any doubt that you will need the engine, leave it running, even if it is sick. Heavy vibration, smoke, blistering paint or a large oil trail, on the other hand, mean a critical failure [[24:283|AFH 13-34]]. In a single that means getting on the ground (application).

head: Clue in cruise
Possible cause
Generic action
rows: Rpm drops (fixed pitch)
Carburetor or induction ice, or a clogged air filter
Carburetor heat, or unfiltered air if available [[24:365|AFH 18-16]]
Airspeed falls with manifold pressure and rpm steady
One or more cylinders may have quit
Land as soon as possible [[24:365|AFH 18-16]]
Fuel pressure drops
Engine-driven pump failure, or no fuel
Boost pump on; switch tanks [[24:365|AFH 18-16]]
Rough running
Wrong mixture, ignition or valve trouble, detonation, induction leak, plugged injector, too much fuel flow
Adjust mixture; reduce power; for detonation, also land as soon as practicable [[24:365|AFH 18-16]]
Rpm surging or overspeed
Propeller, governor, engine, tachometer or mixture
Adjust the propeller control and mixture [[24:365|AFH 18-16]]

body.p: Fuel itself is a common cause. Running a tank dry can let air into the lines and cause vapor lock, which makes a restart hard [[1:186|PHAK 7-26]]. Fuel-injected engines are harder to restart after fuel starvation and can vapor lock on the ground on hot days [[1:172|PHAK 7-12]]. Water in the fuel can freeze and block lines in cold weather, or reach the carburetor and stop the engine in warm weather [[1:187|PHAK 7-27]].

Ignition: each magneto works on its own and fires one of the two plugs in each cylinder. If one magneto fails, the engine keeps running with a slight loss of power [[1:175|PHAK 7-15]]. That is why trying each magneto alone can show which side is bad and whether the engine runs smoother on the other (application).

A partial power loss with a field or airport nearby is a precautionary landing decision. A precautionary landing is less hazardous than a forced one because you still have time and power to correct mistakes; too many pilots let it turn into a forced landing through wishful thinking [[24:350|AFH 18-1]].

callout.text: The engine will not fix itself because you hope it will. Decide early, while you still have power and choices [[24:350|AFH 18-1]].

check.q: In cruise your airspeed is slowly falling but manifold pressure and rpm have not changed. What does the AFH table suggest?
check.a: Possible loss of one or more cylinders. Land as soon as possible [[24:365|AFH 18-16]].

body.p: Fuel evaporating in the venturi, plus the drop in air pressure there, chills the carburetor sharply. Moisture freezes on the venturi and the throttle valve, choking the fuel-air flow and, if enough builds up, stopping the engine [[1:169|PHAK 7-9]].

Ice is most likely below 70 F (21 C) with relative humidity above 80 percent, but it can form at 100 F (38 C) and 50 percent humidity because the temperature inside can drop 60 to 70 F degrees [[1:169|PHAK 7-9]] [[1:170|PHAK 7-10]]. It is especially dangerous at reduced power in a descent, where it can build unnoticed until you add power [[1:170|PHAK 7-10]].

head: Fixed-pitch propeller
Constant-speed propeller
rows: First sign of ice
Rpm drops, then roughness [[1:170|PHAK 7-10]]
Manifold pressure drops; rpm stays the same [[1:170|PHAK 7-10]]
Full heat, ice present
Rpm drops, then slowly rises as ice melts [[1:170|PHAK 7-10]]
Manifold pressure drops, then slowly rises [[1:170|PHAK 7-10]]
Full heat, no ice
Rpm drops and stays steady [[1:170|PHAK 7-10]]
No gradual rise until heat is turned off [[1:170|PHAK 7-10]]

body.p: The fix is full carburetor heat, left on until normal power returns. Partial heat, or heat for too short a time, can make it worse. Expect more roughness for 30 seconds to several minutes as melted ice goes through the engine, and resist the urge to push the heat off [[1:170|PHAK 7-10]]. Heat costs up to about 15 percent of power, so do not use it when you need full power, as on takeoff, except to check for or remove ice [[1:170|PHAK 7-10]] [[1:171|PHAK 7-11]].
A carburetor air temperature gauge, if installed, usually has a yellow arc from -15 C to +5 C. In icing conditions, keep the needle out of the yellow with carburetor heat [[1:171|PHAK 7-11]].

Fuel injection is less prone to icing, but impact ice can still block the air intake. An alternate air source inside the cowling, usually automatic with a manual backup, takes over if the intake is blocked [[1:171|PHAK 7-11]] [[1:172|PHAK 7-12]]. In a carbureted airplane, carburetor heat can serve as alternate air if the filter clogs in airframe icing [[1:170|PHAK 7-10]]. Every airplane must have this kind of propulsion ice protection, even if it is not certificated for icing [[38:32|AC 91-74B 3-13a]].

callout.text: Fuel anti-icing additives are no substitute for carburetor heat [[1:188|PHAK 7-28]].

check.q: You pull full carburetor heat and the engine runs rougher. Do you push the heat back in?
check.a: No. Roughness from melting ice is expected for 30 seconds to several minutes. Leave full heat on until normal power returns [[1:170|PHAK 7-10]].

chunks.title: Heat, detonation, oil and turbocharger trouble

body.p: Detonation is an explosive, uncontrolled burn in the cylinder. It shows as high cylinder head temperature and can quickly ruin pistons, cylinders or valves; milder cases bring overheating, roughness or power loss. Common causes are fuel of a lower grade than specified, very high manifold pressure with low rpm, and high power with a mixture that is too lean [[1:179|PHAK 7-19]]. Forgetting to enrich the mixture while descending from altitude can also lead to it [[1:169|PHAK 7-9]].

Preignition is the mixture lighting early from a hot spot, such as a carbon deposit or a cracked spark plug insulator. It also costs power and raises temperatures. The two often happen together and are hard to tell apart [[1:179|PHAK 7-19]] [[1:180|PHAK 7-20]].

To bring cylinder head temperature down: increase airspeed, enrich the mixture, reduce power, and open cowl flaps if you have them [[1:178|PHAK 7-18]]. Oil temperature reacts slowly and gives only a late, indirect picture of engine heat [[1:178|PHAK 7-18]]. High oil temperature can mean a plugged oil line, low oil, a blocked oil cooler or a bad gauge [[1:177|PHAK 7-17]].

head: Indication
Possible cause
Action (AFH Figure 18-11)
rows: Low oil pressure
Broken relief valve, low oil, burned-out bearings
Land as soon as possible [[24:365|AFH 18-16]]
Fluctuating oil pressure
Low oil supply, loose lines, bad relief valve
Land as soon as possible [[24:365|AFH 18-16]]
High oil temperature
Forthcoming internal failure
Land as soon as possible [[24:365|AFH 18-16]]
High cylinder head temperature
Cowl flaps, low airspeed, mixture, detonation
Adjust cowl flaps, airspeed and mixture; reduce power [[24:365|AFH 18-16]]
Manifold pressure lost in cruise (turbo)
Turbocharger failure; possible exhaust leak
Lowest practical power, or shut down; land as soon as possible [[24:365|AFH 18-16]]

body.p: Turbocharged engines add their own failures. A manual waste gate left closed in a descent can overboost the engine and cause severe detonation, and even an automatic system can overboost if you apply takeoff power with cold oil [[1:174|PHAK 7-14]]. If manifold pressure starts falling below the critical altitude, have the system inspected [[1:175|PHAK 7-15]].

Some newer engines use FADEC, a computer that runs fuel and ignition. A FADEC failure could mean total loss of thrust, so these systems have two identical channels and need a backup electrical source [[1:180|PHAK 7-20]].

check.q: Name three things you can do to lower a high cylinder head temperature.
check.a: Increase airspeed, enrich the mixture, reduce power (and open cowl flaps if equipped) [[1:178|PHAK 7-18]].

body.p: Fire in flight needs immediate, decisive action from the POH procedure. The AFH sorts in-flight fires into engine, electrical and cabin fires [[24:358|AFH 18-9]].

head: Fire
Usual cause and clue
Generic remedy (POH first)
rows: Engine compartment
Fuel, oil or hydraulic fluid on a hot surface; smoke or flames from the cowling, or paint bubbling or melting [[24:358|AFH 18-9]]
Mixture to idle cutoff, fuel selector OFF, ignition left ON to burn the fuel in the lines; never restart [[24:358|AFH 18-9]]
Oil-fed engine fire
Thick black smoke instead of bright orange flames [[24:358|AFH 18-9]]
Consider stopping the propeller (constant-speed: prop control to low rpm, slow down) so the oil pump stops feeding it [[24:358|AFH 18-9]]
Electrical
Smell of burning insulation [[24:359|AFH 18-10]]
Find the bad circuit by breakers, instruments, avionics and lights; if you cannot, and conditions permit, battery master and alternator OFF [[24:359|AFH 18-10]]
Cabin
Smoking, electrical faults or the heater [[24:359|AFH 18-10]]
Shut down the faulty system, use the extinguisher, then open vents to clear smoke [[24:359|AFH 18-10]]

body.p: Turning off the master is not automatic. Unless the fire is electrical or a crash landing is imminent, it costs you the radios for a distress call and ATC loses your transponder [[24:358|AFH 18-9]]. In a single with an engine fire you are headed for a forced landing anyway; treat the airplane as expendable, expect possible structural damage, and know your emergency descent [[24:359|AFH 18-10]]. A fire that seems out can rekindle with changes in airflow and speed [[24:359|AFH 18-10]].

If electrical power is essential, you may try to isolate the bad circuit: master OFF, all switches OFF, master ON, then switches that were on back ON one at a time, pausing to check for smoke or smell. This can recreate the fire, so the prudent course is to land as soon as possible [[24:359|AFH 18-10]]. Materials that already caught fire may keep burning even after the power is off [[24:359|AFH 18-10]].

Clearing smoke: use the extinguisher first, then open the cabin vents. If the smoke gets worse with vents open, close them right away; the fire may be in the heater or nose baggage area, or the airflow is feeding it. Open foul weather windows the same way, use oxygen masks if you have them, and start down. Lowering gear or flaps can make cabin smoke worse in some airplanes [[24:359|AFH 18-10]].

Carbon monoxide comes from an exhaust leak, often through heater or defrost vents, and may be present with no smell. Symptoms include headache, blurred vision, dizziness and drowsiness. Turn the heater off, open fresh air vents and windows, and use oxygen if you have it [[1:434|PHAK 17-12]]. Heater systems can leak exhaust and raise the fire risk, which is why they need careful inspection [[1:189|PHAK 7-29]].

callout.text: An in-flight fire is a serious incident: the operator must notify the nearest NTSB office immediately, even if no one is hurt [[60:882|49 CFR 830.5]].

check.q: Why does the AFH say to leave the ignition ON after shutting off fuel for an engine fire?
check.a: So the engine burns up the fuel still in the lines between the shutoff valve and the engine, which may starve the fire [[24:358|AFH 18-9]].

body.p: Most in-flight electrical failures are in the alternator or generator. After that the battery is your only source, and with one charging system you may have very little time [[24:362|AFH 18-13]]. How long it lasts depends on the load and on the battery's age and charge: a 25 amp-hour battery might give 5 amps for 5 hours, but only about 2 hours at 10 amps, and a 40-amp load could drain it in 10 to 15 minutes [[24:362|AFH 18-13]].

Spot it early. An ammeter needle on the minus side means the battery is supplying more current than it gets back; full-scale minus means the alternator has failed, and full-scale plus points to the voltage regulator. Some airplanes have only a loadmeter or a warning light [[1:191|PHAK 7-31]]. In the schematic, note the split master switch: the ALT half can take the alternator off line and leave everything on the battery [[1:191|PHAK 7-31]].

Then shed load at once and plan to land at the nearest suitable airport [[24:362|AFH 18-13]]. IFH gives a rough 40 minutes of battery, or 30 to 40 minutes of useful voltage, but it says not to rely on that number; never continue the flight after the charging system fails [[23:330|IFH 11-5]]. Pull circuit breakers if you cannot switch items off [[23:330|IFH 11-5]].

If you expect a total failure: shed everything but the essentials, tell ATC now and ask for vectors to the nearest suitable airport, and plan the arrival early, expecting a no-flap landing and a manual gear extension [[24:363|AFH 18-14]]. Gear and flap motors draw so much current that selecting them on a weak battery may cause an immediate total loss [[24:362|AFH 18-13]].

In a glass cockpit the stakes go up. The AHRS, air data computer and displays all need electricity, so losing the alternator, an abnormal event in a round-dial airplane, is an emergency in a technically advanced one [[23:331|IFH 11-6]]. Many have a standby battery that powers the essential bus when the main battery falls to about 19 volts, but only if its switch is in ARM, which should be set before departure [[23:331|IFH 11-6]]. When it is gone, you are left with the standby attitude, altitude and airspeed instruments and the magnetic compass [[23:331|IFH 11-6]].

callout.text: Alternator out: SHED, TELL, LAND. Shed loads, tell ATC, land at the nearest suitable airport, with gear and flaps planned for little or no power [[24:363|AFH 18-14]].
The magnetos do not need the electrical system, so the engine keeps running with a dead battery [[1:175|PHAK 7-15]]. The problem is everything else: radios, lights, flaps, gear and glass displays.

check.q: Why do you plan the gear and flaps early after an alternator failure?
check.a: Their motors draw heavy current; selecting them on a partly drained battery may cause a total electrical loss. Expect a no-flap landing and a manual gear extension [[24:362|AFH 18-13]] [[24:363|AFH 18-14]].

chunks.title: Vacuum failure and the gyro instruments

body.p: In a typical system an engine-driven vacuum pump pulls air through a filter and through the attitude and heading indicators to spin their gyros. A relief valve limits the suction, and a gauge shows it, usually needing about 4.5 to 5.5 inches of mercury [[1:218|PHAK 8-16]]. The same suction may also work pneumatic deice boots [[38:23|AC 91-74B 3-4a]].

When suction drops, the gyros slow down and begin to wander, so the attitude and heading indicators become unstable and wrong [[1:218|PHAK 8-16]] [[1:224|PHAK 8-22]]. The failure is often gradual and silent: many small airplanes have no low-vacuum warning, so the gauge is your only clue [[23:333|IFH 11-8]]. A slowly drifting attitude indicator that you trust can lead you into a dangerous unusual attitude [[23:333|IFH 11-8]].

To find the bad instrument, compare the attitude indicator with the turn indicator and the VSI. That one quick look compares the vacuum system with the electrical and static systems. Then fly on the instruments that still agree, try a backup source, and cover the failed ones [[23:332|IFH 11-7]]. Most airplanes power the turn coordinator electrically so that one power failure still leaves you bank information [[1:218|PHAK 8-16]]. Some have a standby vacuum pump, like the STBY VAC switch in PHAK Figure 7-34 [[1:192|PHAK 7-32]].

If a wandering gyro feeds an autopilot or flight director, they can make wrong control movements too [[23:332|IFH 11-7]]. In VFR conditions, continue visually and land as soon as practicable [[23:333|IFH 11-8]].

callout.text: Make the suction gauge part of every cruise scan. A needle below the green is a failure you can catch before the attitude indicator lies to you [[1:218|PHAK 8-16]].

check.q: Which quick comparison tells you whether the vacuum system or the electrical system has failed?
check.a: Compare the attitude indicator with the turn indicator and the VSI; it cross-checks the vacuum, electrical and static systems [[23:332|IFH 11-7]].

body.p: Ice, dirt, water or insects can block the pitot tube, the static ports or both [[1:212|PHAK 8-10]]. Each blockage has its own fingerprint:

head: Blockage
What the instruments do
rows: Pitot tube blocked, drain hole open
Airspeed falls to zero [[1:212|PHAK 8-10]]
Pitot tube and drain hole blocked
Airspeed stops changing with speed but rises in a climb and falls in a descent [[1:212|PHAK 8-10]] [[1:213|PHAK 8-11]]
Static port blocked
Altimeter freezes, VSI shows zero, airspeed reads low above and high below the blockage altitude [[1:213|PHAK 8-11]]
Static port partly blocked, descending
You look too high, too fast and descending too slowly [[24:364|AFH 18-15]]

body.p: The partial static blockage is the sneaky one: everything can look normal in the takeoff, climb and cruise, and the error appears only in the descent. Climbing again, the airspeed can drop alarmingly close to a stall indication [[24:363|AFH 18-14]] [[24:364|AFH 18-15]]. To confirm, open the alternate static source while climbing or descending. If the needles jump, you had a static problem; keep the alternate source for the rest of the flight [[24:364|AFH 18-15]].

A cabin alternate source has lower pressure than outside, so the altimeter reads higher, the airspeed reads faster, and the VSI briefly shows a climb [[38:29|AC 91-74B 3-11b]]. Check the POH for airspeed corrections [[1:213|PHAK 8-11]]. With no alternate source in an unpressurized airplane, breaking the VSI glass gives the altimeter and airspeed indicator static air, with some added error [[23:333|IFH 11-8]].

Glass cockpits add new failure modes. Many light airplanes feed the backup instruments from the same pitot-static ports as the main display, so one blockage can take out both. Some combine the air data computer and AHRS, so a blockage can even affect the attitude display. Electronic failure indications are not standardized and may look nothing like a round-dial failure [[24:364|AFH 18-15]]. Learn your own system's failure displays [[24:365|AFH 18-16]].

If a screen fails, the system reverts to a composite (reversionary) display on the remaining screen, and the moving map goes away. Keep track of your position on a chart so you still know where the nearest airport is [[23:329|IFH 11-4]]. A red X across the airspeed tape or a blank EFIS needs a POH procedure; you may have to land without airspeed, altitude or vertical speed information [[24:348|AFH 17-14]].

check.q: You suspect a static problem in cruise. When and how does the AFH say to confirm it?
check.a: Open the alternate static source while climbing or descending. If the needles move a lot, it was a static problem; use the alternate source for the rest of the flight [[24:364|AFH 18-15]].

chunks.title: Gear, flaps, flight controls and trim

body.p: Flaps that will not extend mean a no-flap approach. It needs substantially more runway, possibly 50 percent more, and a wider, longer pattern. The nose is higher, which can hide the runway and feel like a stall; avoid diving at the runway, forcing it on fast, or over-flaring into a tail strike [[24:359|AFH 18-10]] [[24:360|AFH 18-11]].

A split flap gives a strong roll toward the wing with less flap. Counter with opposite aileron and lots of opposite rudder, fly the approach faster than normal, fly it onto the runway instead of flaring hard, and do not land with a crosswind from the side of the extended flap [[24:360|AFH 18-11]].

Elevator: a broken up or down cable usually leaves partial pitch control. Lost up elevator: lots of nose-up trim, then push forward and relax pressure to raise the nose and flare. Lost down elevator: the reverse. If the linkage fails completely, the trim tab can move the elevator within limits; a jammed elevator leaves only power and flaps for limited pitch control [[24:360|AFH 18-11]].

Trim: electric trim can run away. Assess it quickly, press the trim disconnect if installed or pull the trim circuit breaker, then hold the pitch force. Depending on the force, you may need a no-flap landing to avoid the flap pitch change [[24:348|AFH 17-14]]. Preflight the trim switch both ways and the disconnect [[24:344|AFH 17-10]]. An autopilot malfunction can also upset the airplane; disengaging it lets you fly directly and may remove the cause [[24:107|AFH 5-2]].

Gear: confirm it really failed. Gear lights that use press-to-test often have interchangeable bulbs, and the gear warning horn cross-checks the lights [[24:243|AFH 12-12]] [[24:248|AFH 12-17]]. Then use the POH alternate extension method, such as free fall, compressed gas or a hand crank [[24:245|AFH 12-14]]. If a leg still will not come down, a gear-up landing is inevitable: pick an airport with crash and rescue, ask for equipment to stand by, prefer a smooth hard runway (but expect sparks), ask about foam, and consider burning off fuel [[24:361|AFH 18-12]].

head: Gear condition
Technique
rows: One main up

Burn fuel from that side; land nose-high, wings level, aileron to hold the wing up; expect a hard yaw, use full opposite rudder and brakes. On a narrow runway with ditches, all gear up may be safer [[24:361|AFH 18-12]]
Nose gear up
Hold the nose off until nearly full up elevator, then let it settle slowly; no brakes unless needed [[24:361|AFH 18-12]]
Only nose gear down
Touch down nose-high on the aft fuselage, then let the nose wheel down gently [[24:362|AFH 18-13]]

callout.text: A flight control system malfunction or failure is a serious incident that must be reported to the NTSB immediately [[60:882|49 CFR 830.5]].

check.q: Electric trim starts running nose-down on its own. What are your first actions?
check.a: Hold the pitch attitude, then stop the trim: press the trim disconnect if installed or pull the trim circuit breaker. Consider a no-flap landing if the forces are high [[24:348|AFH 17-14]].

chunks.title: Inadvertent icing, oxygen and other installed systems

body.p: Most light airplanes have only pitot heat and are not certificated for icing; they must leave icing conditions immediately [[1:200|PHAK 7-40]]. They were never tested for an inadvertent encounter, so their performance in ice is unknown and the FAA recommends getting out as fast as possible [[38:32|AC 91-74B 3-13b]] [[38:32|AC 91-74B 3-13c]]. Do not trust the myth that thick general aviation airfoils tolerate ice; small amounts can raise the stall speed with late or no warning, or stop the climb [[38:32|AC 91-74B 3-13b]].

Ice shows up first as drag: airspeed decays or it takes more power to hold it, and an airplane with little power may approach a stall [[38:23|AC 91-74B 3-3]]. In icing events airspeed has fallen from cruise to stall in under 3 minutes; keep at least 1.5 to 1.6 times the clean stall speed and treat buffet as an imminent stall [[38:48|AC 91-74B 5-7a]]. The stall warning may sound late or not at all [[38:29|AC 91-74B 3-11c]].

The autopilot hides ice. It will hold altitude without regard to airspeed, it can mask the handling changes, and it may disconnect suddenly with an unexpected control deflection. Monitor it closely or hand-fly, and never climb in vertical speed mode in ice, because it holds the rate until the stall [[38:49|AC 91-74B 5-7e]] [[38:49|AC 91-74B 5-7f]] [[38:48|AC 91-74B 5-6d]].

The tail is thinner than the wing and collects ice faster, and you cannot see it. Full flaps increase the tail's down-load angle, and an iced tail can stall and pitch the nose down. Consider a no-flap landing, consistent with the AFM [[38:26|AC 91-74B 3-7a]] [[38:27|AC 91-74B 3-7b]]. With ice on board, carry extra power, limit the flare, avoid slips, and expect a longer landing [[38:52|AC 91-74B 5-10g]] [[38:53|AC 91-74B 5-12e]].

Ice protection systems on certificated airplanes: boots can be cycled as soon as ice is seen, since bridging does not occur with modern boots; thermal anti-ice must be on before you enter ice; and none of it is meant for long exposure [[1:200|PHAK 7-40]] [[1:201|PHAK 7-41]]. An electrically heated windshield can throw the magnetic compass off by as much as 40 degrees [[1:201|PHAK 7-41]].

Oxygen: the required crew must use oxygen above 12,500 ft cabin altitude up to 14,000 ft for the part of the flight there longer than 30 minutes, and for all the time above 14,000 ft; above 15,000 ft every occupant must be provided with it [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211]]. A pressurization failure brings hypoxia; quick use of oxygen and a rapid descent are the answer [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]]. Oxygen makes almost anything burn, so no oil, grease or smoking near it [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]].

check.q: Your airplane is not certificated for icing and you pick up rime ice. What does the FAA recommend, and what speed margin do you protect?
check.a: Exit the icing conditions as fast as possible [[38:32|AC 91-74B 3-13c]], and keep at least 1.5 to 1.6 times the clean stall speed, treating buffet as an imminent stall [[38:48|AC 91-74B 5-7a]].

chunks.title: A door or window opens in flight

body.p: An open door is rarely a threat to the airplane itself. It brings a sudden bang, loud wind noise and maybe buffeting, and the real danger is the pilot who watches the door instead of flying [[24:366|AFH 18-17]].

bullets: Fly the airplane. A door that opens in a light single seldom affects its ability to fly; any roll or yaw is easy to hold [[24:366|AFH 18-17]].
Do not rush back. If it opens after liftoff, climb to pattern altitude, fly a normal pattern and make a normal landing [[24:366|AFH 18-17]].
Stay strapped in. Do not unbuckle to reach the door; close it on the ground [[24:366|AFH 18-17]].
Most doors settle partly open. A slip toward the door may open it wider; a slip away may push it closed [[24:366|AFH 18-17]].
Complete every item on the landing checklist [[24:366|AFH 18-17]].

body.p: Context changes the workload. In VFR an open door should hardly matter; under IFR the same door adds more load, so put it in perspective and prioritize [[1:63|PHAK 2-24]].

callout.text: Accidents almost never come from an open door. They come from a distracted pilot who loses control, often in steep, low turns while hurrying to land [[24:366|AFH 18-17]].

check.q: The cabin door pops open at 200 ft after takeoff. What is the plan?
check.a: Keep flying, climb to pattern altitude, fly a normal pattern and land normally. Stay belted and close the door on the ground [[24:366|AFH 18-17]].

chunks.title: Risk: checklists, distraction, undesired states and startle

body.p: Checklist risk cuts both ways. The approved checklists are a basic defense against errors and undesired aircraft states [[30:46|RMH 6-3]]. But reading a checklist with your head down while the airplane wanders is how a malfunction becomes a loss of control. Do the memory items, keep the airplane under control, then read [[1:234|PHAK 9-4]] [[24:348|AFH 17-14]].

Distraction: many accidents start as a minor problem, such as a gauge not reading right, that pulls attention from flying [[1:63|PHAK 2-24]]. A malfunction can cause an upset simply by diverting your attention [[24:107|AFH 5-2]]. When overloaded, stop, think, slow down and prioritize [[1:63|PHAK 2-24]].

An undesired aircraft state is a wrong position, speed, attitude or configuration, a situation that confuses you and raises workload, or reduced safety margins [[30:46|RMH 6-3]]. Malfunctions such as asymmetric flaps, binding controls and runaway trim can cause one directly [[24:107|AFH 5-2]]. If automation misbehaves, reduce the level of automation and fly manually while you sort it out [[30:51|RMH 7-2]].

Startle is an automatic reflex to a sudden event; surprise is the mental jolt when events break your expectations. Scenario-based training with realistic distractions is how you build resistance to both [[24:108|AFH 5-3]]. Pilots should be able to avoid being startled and make timely decisions [[15:9|AC 61-98E 2.1.2]].

Ask for help early. You are in at least an urgency condition the moment you doubt your position, fuel, weather or anything else that affects safety; that is the time to call, not after it becomes distress [[34:28|AIM 6-1-2]]. Use MAYDAY for distress and PAN-PAN for urgency [[34:45|AIM 6-3-1]].

callout.text: The emergency mindset traps: refusing to accept the situation, panic, and trying to save the airplane at any cost [[24:350|AFH 18-1]] [[24:351|AFH 18-2]].

check.q: What does the AIM say about when to ask for help?
check.a: As soon as you become doubtful about position, fuel, weather or anything affecting safety; you are then in at least an urgency condition [[34:28|AIM 6-1-2]].

chunks.title: On the checkride: three malfunctions, one method

body.p: The examiner will simulate at least three problems from the knowledge list, often by asking, pointing at a gauge or covering an instrument, and wants to see you find and complete the right checklist (ACS CA.IX.C.S1, CA.IX.C.S2). Use the same method every time; this order is our application of the sources:

bullets: Fly: hold attitude, airspeed and heading. In any emergency the most important task is control of the airplane (POH introduction in AFH Figure 17-16) [[24:348|AFH 17-14]].
Identify: name the failure from the clues and cross-checks [[23:332|IFH 11-7]].
Memory items, then checklist: do the immediate actions, then read the POH checklist aloud, item by item [[1:234|PHAK 9-4]].
Decide: continue, land as soon as practicable, or land as soon as possible, and pick the airport or field [[24:365|AFH 18-16]].
Communicate: tell ATC or the CTAF what you have and what you need [[34:45|AIM 6-3-1]].
Brief the landing: configuration, speed and runway for the failure you have [[24:363|AFH 18-14]].

body.p: Talk while you work. Saying 'carburetor ice suspected, full heat, leaving it on' shows the examiner your diagnosis as well as your hands. On a checkride, simulate items like shutting off fuel or the master by touching and naming the control, as agreed in the preflight briefing (application).

callout.text: Before the checkride, find in your own POH: every Section 3 checklist, the abnormal procedures, the alternate gear and flap methods, alternate static and alternate air, and the electrical bus layout. Expect questions on all of them (application).

check.q: What comes before the checklist in every malfunction?
check.a: Keeping control of the airplane, then the memorized immediate action items [[24:348|AFH 17-14]] [[1:234|PHAK 9-4]].

head: Error
Fix
rows: Fixating on the failure and losing altitude or heading
Fly first; airplanes have been lost to fixation on the engine [[24:283|AFH 13-34]]
Partial or brief carburetor heat
Full heat, left on until normal power returns [[1:170|PHAK 7-10]]
Shutting down a sick engine you still need
Leave it running if there is any doubt [[24:283|AFH 13-34]]
Master OFF by reflex for any smoke
Only for an electrical fire or an imminent crash landing; you lose radios and transponder [[24:358|AFH 18-9]]
Waiting after an alternator failure
Shed loads at once and head for the nearest suitable airport [[24:362|AFH 18-13]]
Selecting electric gear or flaps on a weak battery
Plan no-flap and manual gear extension early [[24:363|AFH 18-14]]
Trusting a drifting attitude indicator
Cross-check against the turn indicator and VSI; cover the failed instrument [[23:332|IFH 11-7]]
Unbuckling to close an open door
Stay strapped in; land normally and close it on the ground [[24:366|AFH 18-17]]
Waiting to declare
Ask for help at the first doubt [[34:28|AIM 6-1-2]]

check.q: What is the most common thread in these errors?
check.a: Letting the malfunction take attention from flying the airplane [[24:107|AFH 5-2]] [[24:283|AFH 13-34]].

A primary bus and an avionics bus run down the right, each feeding labeled circuit breakers for items such as pitot heat, wing flaps, landing lights, the turn coordinator and the radios.

scenario.title: Ice, an autopilot and a lying altimeter
scenario.setup: You hold a commercial certificate with an instrument rating and are flying a fuel-injected single that is not certificated for flight in icing. It has a glass PFD, a two-axis autopilot, pitot heat, an alternate static source, and standby airspeed and altimeter that share the main pitot-static ports. You are IFR at 8,000 ft in cloud, OAT -4 C, autopilot holding altitude, with one passenger. Rime ice appears on the leading edges and the windshield frame, and in two minutes your airspeed has dropped 10 knots at the same power.

questions.a: Get out of the ice now: an airplane not certificated for icing must avoid it and exit immediately if it is encountered inadvertently [[38:32|AC 91-74B 3-13b]]. Ask ATC for a lower or higher altitude or a turn back to clear air, and say why; doubt about safety already makes this at least an urgency situation [[34:28|AIM 6-1-2]]. Turn pitot heat on if it is not already; even light ice can block the pitot tube [[38:28|AC 91-74B 3-11a]].

questions.q: The autopilot is still holding 8,000 ft. What is the hidden danger?
questions.a: It holds altitude without regard to airspeed, so as ice adds drag it will keep raising the nose toward a stall, and it masks the handling changes you would feel. It may also disconnect suddenly with an unexpected control deflection [[38:49|AC 91-74B 5-7e]] [[38:49|AC 91-74B 5-7f]]. Watch airspeed and pitch closely or hand-fly, and do not use vertical speed mode [[38:48|AC 91-74B 5-6d]].

questions.q: Your clean stall speed is 60 KIAS. What minimum speed do you protect, and what do you make of buffet?
questions.a: At least 1.5 x 60 = 90 KIAS (1.6 x 60 = 96 KIAS for more margin), and treat any buffet or shudder as an imminent wing stall [[38:48|AC 91-74B 5-7a]]. Do not count on the stall warning; ice can make the wing stall before it sounds [[38:29|AC 91-74B 3-11c]].

questions.q: Cleared down to 4,000 ft, you see the PFD altitude and the standby altimeter both lagging, both airspeeds reading high, and a very small descent rate on the VSI. What is happening and what do you do?
questions.a: A partly blocked static source, likely ice; you look too high, too fast and descending too slowly [[24:364|AFH 18-15]]. Both instruments agree because they share the same ports [[24:364|AFH 18-15]]. Open the alternate static source while descending; if the needles move, keep it on [[24:364|AFH 18-15]]. Expect the altimeter and airspeed to read a bit high and the VSI to blip up [[38:29|AC 91-74B 3-11b]], and use the POH corrections [[1:213|PHAK 8-11]].

questions.q: You break out below the cloud with ice still on the leading edges. How do you plan the approach and landing?
questions.a: Expect a higher stall speed and add speed per the POH [[38:52|AC 91-74B 5-11a]]. Be wary of full flaps, which can stall an iced tail; consider a no-flap landing if the AFM allows [[38:27|AC 91-74B 3-7b]]. Avoid slips, carry extra power, limit the flare and plan for a longer runway [[38:53|AC 91-74B 5-12e]] [[38:52|AC 91-74B 5-10g]].

questions.q: Your passenger is alarmed and keeps asking questions while you troubleshoot. How do you manage it?
questions.a: Prioritize: fly, then troubleshoot, then talk. Overload makes pilots work harder and achieve less; stop, think, slow down and prioritize [[1:63|PHAK 2-24]]. A passenger can be given a simple task, such as watching for traffic or holding the checklist, if it helps [[30:46|RMH 6-3]]. Let ATC help too [[34:28|AIM 6-1-2]].

skills.do: The examiner gives you at least three simulated emergencies from the Task's knowledge list (for example power loss, an alternator failure, a static blockage, smoke). For each, you keep the airplane under control, name the likely cause from the clues, and state and take the right action. The ACS gives no numerical tolerance here; control and correct action are what count.
skills.practice: Have your CFI give you surprise failures in cruise: cover an instrument, call out 'smell of burning insulation', or set up a high cylinder head temperature. Say aloud fly, identify, memory items, checklist, decide, communicate [[24:348|AFH 17-14]] [[23:332|IFH 11-7]].

skills.do: You find and complete the appropriate POH checklist for each malfunction, doing memory items first and then reading the checklist item by item without losing control of the airplane.
skills.practice: Tab or mark the Section 3 checklists so you can open each in seconds. Practice the memory items on the ground until they are automatic, then read the checklist in flight [[1:234|PHAK 9-4]].

quiz.q: What is an optional Abnormal Procedures subsection of the POH for?
options: Malfunctions that are not considered emergencies
Procedures for optional equipment
Maneuvers that are prohibited
Weight and balance changes
quiz.why: Manufacturers may add an Abnormal Procedures subsection to Section 3 for malfunctions that are not emergencies [[1:234|PHAK 9-4]]. Optional equipment goes in Section 9, Supplements [[1:235|PHAK 9-5]].

quiz.q: In cruise, airspeed drops while manifold pressure and rpm stay constant. What does AFH Figure 18-11 suggest?
options: Carburetor ice; apply heat
Possible loss of one or more cylinders; land as soon as possible
A defective tachometer; consult maintenance
Turbocharger overboost; reduce throttle
quiz.why: That indication points to a possible loss of one or more cylinders, and the action is to land as soon as possible [[24:365|AFH 18-16]]. Carburetor ice shows as a loss of rpm or manifold pressure [[1:170|PHAK 7-10]].

quiz.q: A carburetor air temperature gauge typically has a yellow arc covering:
options: 0 C to +15 C
-15 C to +5 C
-5 C to +15 C
-30 C to 0 C
quiz.why: The yellow arc usually runs from -15 C to +5 C (5 F to 41 F); in icing conditions keep the needle out of it with carburetor heat [[1:171|PHAK 7-11]].

options: Fuel of a lower grade than specified
A residual hot spot such as a carbon deposit or a cracked plug insulator
Too rich a mixture at altitude
A failed magneto
quiz.why: Preignition comes from a hot spot in the combustion chamber that lights the charge early [[1:179|PHAK 7-19]]. Low-grade fuel is a classic cause of detonation [[1:179|PHAK 7-19]].

quiz.q: In a glass cockpit with a standby battery, when does the standby battery normally take over the essential bus?
options: As soon as the alternator fails, whatever the switch position
When the main battery falls to about 19 volts, if its switch is in ARM
Only when the pilot turns the master switch OFF in flight
When the PFD goes into reversionary mode
quiz.why: It comes online at about 19 volts on the main battery, but generally only if the standby battery switch is in ARM, which should be set before departure [[23:331|IFH 11-6]].

quiz.q: How does the AFH say to confirm a suspected static system problem?
options: Tap the altimeter in level flight
Open the alternate static source while climbing or descending
Turn the pitot heat on and off
Compare the GPS altitude with the altimeter in cruise
quiz.why: Open the alternate static source while climbing or descending; if the needles move significantly, a static problem exists and you keep the alternate source [[24:364|AFH 18-15]].

quiz.q: If you must land with only the nose gear extended, where should initial contact be made?
options: On the nose wheel, with the tail held high
On the aft fuselage, nose-high, then let the nose wheel down
On the wing tip, to slow down evenly
Flat, with the fuselage and nose wheel together
quiz.why: Touch down on the aft fuselage in a nose-high attitude to prevent porpoising or wheelbarrowing, then let the nose wheel down gradually [[24:362|AFH 18-13]].

quiz.q: What side effect of an electrically heated windshield does the PHAK warn about?
options: It weakens the static ports
It can cause magnetic compass errors of up to 40 degrees
It drains the vacuum pump
It disables the stall warning
quiz.why: The current in the windshield can cause compass deviation errors of as much as 40 degrees, and it should not be left on during ground operations [[1:201|PHAK 7-41]].

quiz.q: How does the AFH define startle?
options: A planned reaction practiced in training
An uncontrollable, automatic reflex with raised heart rate to a sudden, intense, unexpected event
A slow loss of situational awareness
The fear of damaging the airplane
quiz.why: Startle is an automatic muscle reflex with raised heart rate and blood pressure; surprise is the mental reaction to an event that violates expectations [[24:108|AFH 5-3]].

quiz.q: What is usually the first sign of an electrical fire?
options: A flickering ammeter
The distinct odor of burning insulation
Black smoke from the cowling
A popped circuit breaker
quiz.why: The initial indication is usually the smell of burning insulation [[24:359|AFH 18-10]]. Black smoke from the cowling suggests an oil-fed engine fire [[24:358|AFH 18-9]].

final_quiz.q: Humid day, 60 F, fixed-pitch prop. Rpm sags in cruise. You pull full carburetor heat; rpm drops further and the engine runs rough for 40 seconds. What now?
options: Push the heat off; it is making things worse
Use half heat as a compromise
Leave full heat on until normal power returns
Lean the mixture to full lean to smooth it
final_quiz.why: Roughness from melted ice can last 30 seconds to several minutes, and partial heat can aggravate icing. Leave full heat on until power returns [[1:170|PHAK 7-10]].

final_quiz.q: After a long cruise at high altitude you start a power-on descent without touching the mixture. CHT climbs and the engine runs rough. What is the best explanation and fix?
options: Carburetor ice; full heat
The mixture is now too lean, inviting detonation; enrich, reduce power, add airspeed
A failed magneto; switch to BOTH
Spark plug fouling from a rich mixture; lean further
final_quiz.why: Descending without enriching can make the mixture too lean and cause detonation [[1:169|PHAK 7-9]]. Lower CHT by enriching, reducing power and increasing airspeed [[1:178|PHAK 7-18]].

final_quiz.q: Your turbocharged airplane has a manual waste gate. You start a long descent from altitude and forget to open it. What is the risk?
options: Overboost and severe detonation
Loss of manifold pressure
Carburetor ice
Vapor lock
final_quiz.why: A closed manual waste gate in a descent can overboost the engine, with severe detonation from the leaning effect of denser air [[1:174|PHAK 7-14]].

final_quiz.q: You smell burning insulation in IMC and cannot find the bad circuit, but you need the radios to get down. What does the AFH allow, and what is the catch?
options: Nothing; the master must stay off until landing
Master off, all switches off, master on, then needed switches on one at a time watching for smoke; it may recreate the fire, so land as soon as possible
Leave everything on and open the vents
Pull every circuit breaker and reset them together
final_quiz.why: If power is essential, isolate the circuit that way, pausing after each switch. It can recreate the original problem, so land as soon as possible [[24:359|AFH 18-10]].

final_quiz.q: In a glass-cockpit single the alternator fails one hour from your destination; a suitable airport is 20 minutes away. Best plan?
options: Continue; the standby battery covers an hour
Shed load, tell ATC and land at the nearby airport
Turn everything off and fly home on the magnetos
Keep the load on so the standby battery stays charged
final_quiz.why: Never continue after the charging system fails; battery time is uncertain and in a glass cockpit this is an emergency [[23:330|IFH 11-5]] [[23:331|IFH 11-6]]. Shed load and land at the nearest suitable airport [[24:362|AFH 18-13]].

final_quiz.q: Your PFD goes black in cruise. What should you expect from a G1000-type system?
options: Everything is lost until you reset the system
A reversionary display on the remaining screen with flight and engine data, but no moving map
The autopilot takes over and lands
Only the standby compass remains
final_quiz.why: The system reverts to a composite reversionary mode that drops the moving map, which is why you keep track of position on a chart [[23:329|IFH 11-4]].

final_quiz.q: A gear leg will not extend by any method. Which runway choice does the AFH lean toward, and what precaution goes with it?
options: Rough grass, because it is softer and cannot spark
A smooth hard runway, which usually does less damage, but sparks can ignite fuel, so ask about foam and consider burning off fuel
Water, to avoid fire
Any runway, as long as the approach is fast
final_quiz.why: A smooth hard surface usually causes less damage than a rough grass strip, but sparks can ignite fuel; request foam if available, burn off fuel, and ask for emergency equipment [[24:361|AFH 18-12]].

final_quiz.q: The up-elevator cable breaks on final. You have trimmed nose-up and are holding forward pressure. How do you flare?
options: Pull back on the yoke
Release forward pressure
Add full nose-down trim
Lower full flaps at the threshold
final_quiz.why: With the up cable gone, you control pitch with forward pressure against nose-up trim, and you flare by releasing that forward pressure [[24:360|AFH 18-11]].

final_quiz.q: A cabin door pops open on climbout and settles partly open. Which control input might help it close?
options: A slip toward the door
A slip away from the door
A steep turn toward the door
Full flaps
final_quiz.why: A slip toward the door may open it wider, and a slip away from it may push it closed. Keep flying and land normally [[24:366|AFH 18-17]].

final_quiz.q: Climbing on autopilot in vertical speed mode to get above a cloud deck, you pick up ice in a non-icing-certificated airplane. Why is this especially dangerous?
options: Vertical speed mode turns pitot heat off
The autopilot holds the climb rate as ice builds until the airplane stalls
Vertical speed mode disables the stall warning
It causes carburetor ice
final_quiz.why: As ice reduces climb performance, the autopilot keeps the commanded rate until stall; climbing in vertical speed mode in icing is highly discouraged [[38:48|AC 91-74B 5-6d]]. Exit the ice instead [[38:32|AC 91-74B 3-13c]].

final_quiz.q: After flying through ice, you select full flaps on final and right away feel buffeting and the nose pitches down hard. What does this suggest?
options: Normal flap pitch change
A possible ice-contaminated tailplane stall, so a no-flap landing should be considered
Carburetor ice
A split flap
final_quiz.why: An iced tail can stall after full flap extension and pitch the nose down; a no-flap landing should be considered, consistent with the AFM [[38:27|AC 91-74B 3-7b]] [[38:52|AC 91-74B 5-12a]]. Buffet without a recent full-flap selection should be treated as a wing stall [[38:52|AC 91-74B 5-12b]].

final_quiz.q: Your unpressurized airplane is at a cabin altitude of 15,500 ft. What does 14 CFR 91.211 require?
options: Only the pilot must use oxygen after 30 minutes
The required crew must use oxygen the entire time above 14,000 ft, and every occupant must be provided with oxygen
Every occupant must wear a mask
Nothing, if the flight is under 30 minutes
final_quiz.why: Above 14,000 ft the required crew must use oxygen the whole time, and above 15,000 ft each occupant must be provided with it; provided does not mean passengers must use it [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211]].

final_quiz.q: Fuel flow becomes erratic and you are unsure your fuel will last to destination. What does the AIM say about your situation?
options: Nothing is needed until the engine stops
You are in at least an urgency condition now; ask for help, using PAN-PAN
Only a distress call is allowed
You must squawk 7600
final_quiz.why: Doubt about fuel endurance puts you in at least an urgency condition; that is the time to ask for help [[34:28|AIM 6-1-2]]. PAN-PAN signals urgency [[34:45|AIM 6-3-1]].

takeaways: Fly the airplane first; most malfunction accidents come from distraction, not the failure.
The POH wins: memory items, then the Section 3 checklist, abnormal procedures and supplements.
Partial power: orderly check of fuel, air, mixture, magnetos and boost pump; leave a sick engine running if you might need it.
Carburetor ice needs full heat, left on until power returns, even through the roughness.
Fire: fuel off and ignition on for engine fire; master off only for electrical fire; vents only after the extinguisher.
Alternator out: shed, tell, land, with no-flap and manual gear planned early.
Not certificated for ice means exit now, protect 1.5 to 1.6 times stall speed, and watch the autopilot.
cfi_notes: The private and commercial ACS list identical elements for this Task (PA.IX.C and CA.IX.C). Raise the bar through depth: make the commercial applicant explain the system behind each checklist step in the airplane they will use on the test.

The AFH's best list of power-loss troubleshooting steps (tanks, carburetor heat or alternate air, one magneto, mixture, boost pump, and 'leave it running if in doubt') sits in the multiengine chapter [[24:283|AFH 13-34]]. The steps are generic and apply to singles, but point out where they come from.

The PHAK oxygen summary says crews need oxygen 'after 30 minutes' between 12,500 and 14,000 ft and that every occupant above 15,000 ft 'must have' it [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]]. Teach the rule text: required crew use it for the part of the flight there that lasts more than 30 minutes, and occupants above 15,000 ft must be provided with it [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211]].
AIM 6-1-1 says the emergency authority covers Part 91 Subparts A and B [[34:28|AIM 6-1-1]], while 14 CFR 91.3(b) says any rule of Part 91 [[60:435|14 CFR 91.3]]. Teach the regulation.

The IFH gives two battery numbers: about 40 minutes (30 to 40 of useful voltage) [[23:330|IFH 11-5]] and 'up to 45 minutes or only minutes' [[23:331|IFH 11-6]]. The AFH battery example shows why: higher loads drain a battery faster than simple division suggests [[24:362|AFH 18-13]]. The lesson is not a number but 'land now'.

Several sources here come from other chapters: trim runaway from the light-sport chapter [[24:348|AFH 17-14]], icing from AC 91-74B, which is written partly with larger airplanes in mind. Keep the student focused on what applies to their airplane and POH.

Simulate failures realistically but safely: cover instruments, call out smells, or describe a gauge reading. Never actually shut off fuel or the master in flight for training unless the POH and the situation allow it (application).

Build startle resistance by giving failures without warning in scenarios that carry some pressure, as the AFH suggests [[24:108|AFH 5-3]]; a student who only gets malfunctions on cue has never been startled.
gaps: Every specific step, switch name and speed for your airplane's malfunctions (alternator reset, gear free-fall or hand-crank method, alternate air, trim disconnect, standby battery) is in the POH/AFM, not in the handbooks.

The sources give no numbers for how long your specific battery will last; that depends on its rating, age and the load, and only the POH electrical load data and testing can tell you [[24:362|AFH 18-13]].

No FAA source here gives a procedure for ice-contaminated tailplane stall recovery in a light single beyond following the AFM and considering a no-flap landing [[38:27|AC 91-74B 3-7b]]. Ask a CFI and read the AFM.
Electronic display failure indications are not standardized, and the handbooks cannot show your system's version; use the avionics manufacturer's guide [[24:364|AFH 18-15]].
The sources do not say how an examiner must simulate fires or switch failures in flight; agree on 'touch and name' simulation in the preflight briefing.

activities.title: True or false: smoke and fire
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: Bright orange flames suggest a fuel-fed engine fire; thick black smoke suggests an oil-fed one.
cards.why: True. The AFH contrasts the bright orange flames of a fuel-fed fire with the thick black smoke of an oil-fed fire [[24:358|AFH 18-9]].

cards.s: If the engine fire goes out after you shut off the fuel, restart the engine to reach a better field.
cards.why: False. If the flames are snuffed out, no attempt should be made to restart the engine [[24:358|AFH 18-9]].

cards.s: For cabin smoke, open the vents first and then use the extinguisher.
cards.why: False. Use the extinguisher first, then open the vents to purge smoke [[24:359|AFH 18-10]].

cards.s: If smoke gets worse when you open the vents, close them right away.
cards.why: True. It may mean a fire in the heater or nose baggage area, or that the airflow is feeding the fire [[24:359|AFH 18-10]].

cards.s: In some airplanes, lowering the gear or flaps can make a cabin smoke problem worse.
cards.why: True. The AFH warns of this [[24:359|AFH 18-10]].

cards.s: Turning off the battery master and alternator guarantees an electrical fire will go out.
cards.why: False. It removes the likely source, but materials that already caught fire may keep burning [[24:359|AFH 18-10]].

cards.s: No exhaust smell in the cabin means no carbon monoxide.
cards.why: False. CO can be present in dangerous amounts with no exhaust odor [[1:434|PHAK 17-12]].

cards.s: An in-flight fire must be reported to the NTSB immediately, even with no injuries or damage.
cards.why: True. In-flight fire is one of the serious incidents that require immediate notification [[60:882|49 CFR 830.5]].

activities.title: Work the malfunction numbers
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer.

items.q: The temperature inside a carburetor can drop as much as 70 F degrees. Outside air is 90 F. How cold could the carburetor get?
items.why: 90 - 70 = 20 F, well below freezing, so ice is possible on a hot day [[1:169|PHAK 7-9]] [[1:170|PHAK 7-10]].

items.q: Convert that 70 F degree drop into Celsius degrees (there are 180 F degrees and 100 C degrees between freezing and boiling).
Your clean stall speed is 58 KIAS. In icing, AC 91-74B says to keep at least 1.5 times it. What is the minimum?
items.why: 1.5 x 58 = 87 KIAS (1.6 x 58 = 92.8 KIAS for the upper margin) [[38:48|AC 91-74B 5-7a]].

items.q: Light icing is up to about 1 inch per hour on the unprotected outer wing. At that top rate, how much ice builds in 25 minutes?
items.why: 1 x 25 / 60 = 0.42 in [[38:39|AC 91-74B 4-2b]]. Even that much rough ice can raise the stall speed [[38:32|AC 91-74B 3-13b]].

items.q: A portable oxygen bottle lasts 2 hours with continuous flow. A pulse-demand system can cut oxygen use by 50 to 85 percent. At the low end (50 percent), how long would the same bottle last?
items.why: Using half the oxygen doubles the time: 2 / (1 - 0.50) = 4 hours [[1:199|PHAK 7-39]].

activities.title: Rough engine on a photo flight, one decision at a time
activities.intro: You are flying a fuel-injected, retractable single on a paid aerial photo flight at 3,500 ft AGL on a hot afternoon after a long climb. A photographer is aboard. A nontowered airport is 10 miles away; your home base is 45 minutes away.

steps.s: The engine starts running rough and the fuel flow needle is jumping.
options: Shut the engine down before it damages itself
Keep flying at a safe speed and run an orderly check of fuel, air, mixture, magnetos and boost pump
Pull the mixture to idle cutoff to reset it
Turn back toward home right away and troubleshoot later
steps.why: Many power problems can be fixed with an orderly check of switches and gauges, while you keep control of the airplane [[24:283|AFH 13-34]]. Leave the engine running if you might need it [[24:283|AFH 13-34]].

steps.s: Tanks and mixture are fine. A hot day and a long climb make you suspect fuel vapor.
options: Turn on the boost pump
Switch to alternate air
Switch to one magneto
Reduce to idle
steps.why: If fuel vapor is suspected, boost pump operation may eliminate the flow and pressure fluctuations [[24:283|AFH 13-34]]. Fuel-injected engines are prone to vapor problems on hot days [[1:172|PHAK 7-12]].

steps.s: The engine smooths out but still is not making full power.
options: Finish the photo run, then go home
Make a precautionary landing at the airport 10 miles away
Circle and keep troubleshooting until it is perfect
Shut it down to save the engine
steps.why: A precautionary landing while you still have power is less hazardous than letting it become a forced landing; developing engine trouble is a classic reason for one [[24:350|AFH 18-1]].

steps.s: On downwind you select gear down. You get two green lights; the nose gear light stays dark.
options: Land; it is probably just a bulb
Press-to-test or swap the bulb and cross-check the gear horn, then use the POH alternate extension if needed
Cycle the gear up and down until it works
Pull the gear circuit breaker
steps.why: Confirm the indication first: press-to-test bulbs are often interchangeable, and the horn cross-checks the lights [[24:243|AFH 12-12]] [[24:248|AFH 12-17]]. If the gear is really not down, use the POH alternate method [[24:245|AFH 12-14]].

steps.s: The bulb is good and the alternate extension fails; the nose gear is still up. The engine is running steadily.
options: Retract the mains and land wheels up
Land on the mains, hold the nose off until nearly full up elevator, then let it settle slowly with no brakes
Land fast and hold full up elevator all the way
Fly home to your mechanic
steps.why: With the mains down and locked, hold the nose off until almost full up elevator, then release back pressure so it settles slowly; holding full up elevator lets it drop abruptly. Avoid braking and ask for emergency equipment [[24:361|AFH 18-12]].
